tldr: In real-world online reinforcement learning, by coordinating continuous arm motion and discrete gripper opening/closing via centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), and introducing a multi-head critic with reward decomposition into task and grasp heads (HRA), this approach achieves high sample efficiency and success rates even under 5-25x larger initial position randomization ranges compared to prior work.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed method HARC. Built on a data accumulation pipeline with human intervention (RLPD), it integrates a CTDE structure that evaluates both arm and gripper actions via a centralized critic, alongside a multi-head critic that splits sparse task reward and dense grasping reward.
overview:
Real-world online reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising approach for training robotic manipulation policies directly in the physical world, avoiding the sim-to-real gap while continuously refining skills through human-in-the-loop (HIL) interactions. However, existing methods (such as SERL) remain limited to very small workspace initial position variations of just a few centimeters, presenting major challenges for generalizing to diverse real-world situations and executing long-horizon tasks.

Furthermore, real-world robotic manipulation must handle a hybrid action space: a continuously moving arm alongside a discrete-action gripper (e.g., open/close). Handling this with a single policy creates difficult-to-optimize decision boundaries. Conversely, training two policies independently with separate rewards causes each agent's policy updates to appear as environmental non-stationarity to the other, severely destabilizing learning. In addition, real-world camera image noise tends to cause exploding critic gradients.

To tackle these issues, the authors propose "HARC," a method combining centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)—a concept from multi-agent reinforcement learning—with a Hybrid Reward Architecture (HRA) that decomposes rewards to reduce estimation difficulty. During training, actions from both agents are evaluated together by a centralized multi-head critic, while execution remains decentralized during inference. Furthermore, rewards are split into a sparse overall task completion reward and a dense potential-based grasping reward, each learned by distinct critic heads.

Using two real-world robot arms and a simulated humanoid robot, experiments were conducted under domain randomization ranges 5 to 25 times larger than prior work. The results demonstrated that across tasks including tennis ball and banana pick-and-place, pot reset, and block relocation, HARC significantly outperformed the state-of-the-art baseline (HIL-SERL) in both sample efficiency and success rate, achieving practical robustness with roughly 2.5 hours of real-world training.
contributions: Resolved the non-stationarity issue by establishing a CTDE framework that separates continuous Cartesian arm control from discrete gripper control while training them via a centralized critic.

Dramatically stabilized value estimation under noisy real-world RGB camera observations using an HRA structure that decomposes rewards into task completion and grasp potential learned through separate critic heads.

Demonstrated consistently high performance and sample efficiency across multiple tasks spanning two real-world robot arms and a simulated humanoid robot under large-scale domain randomization 5-25x wider than prior work.
Developed and integrated a compliant gripper with passive adaptability that enables both fingertip and enveloping grasps without additional actuators.

sections.heading: The Double Bottleneck in Real-World Online RL: Limited Randomization and Hybrid Actions
sections.summary: While real-world online RL is a promising route to circumvent the sim-to-real gap, prior methods were confined to extremely narrow exploration ranges. Furthermore, hybrid action spaces mixing continuous arm movements with discrete gripper commands, alongside critic instability caused by camera image noise, posed significant hurdles.
sections.details:
When a policy trained in simulation is transferred to a real robot, performance often degrades significantly due to discrepancies in dynamics, contact physics, and sensor noise. To bypass this sim-to-real gap, online reinforcement learning directly on physical hardware—with human teleoperation intervention (Human-in-the-loop: HIL)—has drawn considerable attention.

However, existing representative approaches (such as SERL and HIL-SERL) have only been verified in narrow workspaces with initial position variations of just a few centimeters and fixed camera viewpoints. Building policies that are genuinely useful in realistic environments requires withstanding large-scale domain randomization where objects move across much wider spatial extents.

This introduces two technical roadblocks. The first is handling the hybrid action space, where continuous Cartesian pose control of the arm is combined with discrete open/close commands for the gripper. Forcing a single policy to solve this induces discontinuous boundaries, whereas splitting into two separate policies trained independently destabilizes value estimation, as each agent's updates act as environmental non-stationarity to the other.

The second issue stems from lighting variations and background noise in real-world RGB images. Unlike simulation, real camera noise is substantial. Under sparse reward settings (where rewards are given only upon task success), attempting to regress long-term returns through a single critic network leads to severe gradient variance. To overcome these challenges, the authors proposed a unified framework integrating centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) and critic decomposition (HRA).

sections.heading: Lineage of Related Work: Real-World Online RL and Hybrid Action Spaces
sections.summary: Although real-world online RL based on frameworks like RLPD has progressed, it remains confined to narrow operational ranges. Moreover, attempts to address mixed continuous-discrete control via action discretization or continuous relaxation have proven insufficient for high-precision physical grasping.
sections.details:
This work builds on two main research areas:

- **Real-world online reinforcement learning**: Frameworks such as SERL and HIL-SERL have been introduced based on RLPD, which efficiently mixes offline demonstrations with online interactions. While showing that complex contact-rich tasks can be mastered in hours of training, their evaluation environments were restricted to minimal randomization ranges of only 2 to 8 cm. Expanding the workspace causes an explosion in exploration space; under limited human intervention budgets, learning solely from sparse rewards breaks down.

- **Hybrid action spaces and multi-agent RL**: Manipulation inherently requires both continuous positioning and discrete grasping. Prior studies have attempted either discretizing the entire action space or relaxing discrete actions into continuous values. However, the former degrades positioning precision, while the latter blurs binary "firmly grasp/release" decisions. Attempts to employ independent policies for the arm and gripper also fail, as decentralized learning breaks the stationarity assumption of Markov Decision Processes.

This work introduces Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE)—a proven concept in multi-agent RL—to preserve the benefits of decentralized inference while fundamentally eliminating non-stationarity during training.

sections.heading: HARC: Fast and Stable Learning via Centralized Critic and Reward Decomposition
sections.summary: HARC uses RLPD as its backbone, separating policies into continuous SAC for the arm and discrete SAC for the gripper, with both evaluated jointly by a centralized critic. Furthermore, the critic is split into task-completion and grasp-potential heads, and paired with a passively compliant gripper.
sections.details:
The overall architecture and core mechanisms of the proposed "HARC" (Hybrid Actors with a Reward-decomposed Critic) framework are as follows:

- **III-A: Sample-efficient RL leveraging prior data**
The foundation is built on SAC (Soft Actor-Critic) and the RLPD algorithm. The replay buffer maintains a Policy buffer (holding autonomous attempts and human interventions) alongside a Demo buffer (containing prior teleoperated demonstrations), sampling evenly at 50% from each per minibatch. A high Update-To-Data (UTD) ratio, which updates the critic multiple times per collected step, is employed to maximize sample efficiency.

- **III-B: Coordinating hybrid action spaces via CTDE**
Arm control $\pi_\phi^c$ is modeled via continuous SAC, while gripper control $\pi_\psi^d$ is completely decoupled as discrete SAC outputting a categorical distribution. The discrete SAC architecture outputs Q-values for all actions simultaneously to enhance computational efficiency. During execution, each agent selects actions independently using local observations (e.g., wrist camera for the gripper, wrist plus overhead camera for the arm). During training, however, a centralized critic receives both actions $(a_c, a_d)$ to evaluate joint performance, eliminating non-stationarity caused by unobserved partner actions.

- **III-C: Critic decomposition via HRA (Hybrid Reward Architecture)**
Real-world RGB image noise is substantial; regressing the entire long-term return through a single massive Q-function causes high TD error variance. To mitigate this, the reward is decomposed into a sparse overall achievement reward $r_{\mathrm{task}}$ and a dense potential-based reward (PBRS) $r_{\mathrm{grasp}}$ derived from gripper width and grasp torque. While sharing lower-level backbone features inside the critic, separate task and grasp heads are instantiated. Simplifying the regression target for each head stabilizes critic gradients against visual noise, dramatically accelerating convergence.

- **III-D: Compliant gripper for enveloping diverse geometries**
Innovations were also introduced on the hardware side. A passively compliant gripper was developed combining a single-DOF rotary actuator with tendon-driven transmission and elastic elements. For small objects, it locks against mechanical stoppers to perform rigid fingertip grasps; for larger or irregularly shaped objects, the joints bend passively into enveloping grasps. From the RL controller's perspective, it remains a simple 1-DOF open/close command, drastically improving physical grasp reliability without expanding the RL action space.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Dominant Success Rates Under 5-25x Wider Randomization
sections.summary: Evaluated across two physical arms and a humanoid robot under pose randomization 5 to 25 times wider than prior studies. HARC raised the average real-world success rate from 40% (baseline) to 75% in about 2.5 hours of physical training, and achieved a dramatic improvement from 25% to 95% in simulation.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated HARC against the state-of-the-art baseline, "HIL-SERL." Both methods started with only 20 initial demonstrations and ran for approximately 2.5 hours (160 minutes) of wall-clock online training on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Notably, while the original HIL-SERL paper tested randomizations of roughly $2\sim 8\,\mathrm{cm}$, this benchmark expanded initial object variation by 5 to 25 times per dimension (e.g., $50\times 40\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $360^\circ$ rotations).

- **Task Setups and Complexity**
1. *Tennis ball pick-and-place (Custom real arm)*: Pick a ball within a $50\times 40\,\mathrm{cm}$ area and place it at a target. Missed grasps cause the ball to roll away, requiring dynamic recovery.
2. *Banana pick-and-place (Custom real arm + compliant gripper)*: Random placement within $30\times 30\,\mathrm{cm}$ with $360^\circ$ yaw variation. Requires precise approach angles due to asymmetric geometry.
3. *Pot reset (Real Franka arm)*: $40\times 40\,\mathrm{cm}$ area, up to $90^\circ$ rotation. Severe specular reflection noise on the metal surface; requires precise gripping of flat elliptical handles.
4. *Two-block relocation (Simulated Unitree G1 humanoid)*: A long-horizon task sequentially transferring two cubes of different sizes into a box. Blocks are frequently occluded by the robot's own arm during transport.

- **Performance and Sample Efficiency Comparisons**
Across 20 evaluation episodes, HARC boosted success rates from 60% to 80% on tennis ball pick-and-place, and from 60% to 90% on banana pick-and-place. Across the three physical robot tasks, average success doubled from 40% to 75%. Most strikingly, on the humanoid block relocation task where the baseline largely failed at 25%, HARC reached an impressive **95%** success rate.

Furthermore, the amount of human intervention required during training (measured in demonstration-equivalent episodes) dropped significantly: from 80 to 69 on tennis ball, and from 189 down to 115 on block relocation. Thanks to the centralized critic and reward decomposition, the policy acquired recovery behaviors much faster with substantially less human assistance.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Toward Practical Real-World Manipulation RL
sections.summary: Combining CTDE with HRA significantly boosts learning efficiency for physical manipulation under hybrid action spaces and severe domain randomization. Future work aims to scale this approach to bimanual coordination on humanoid robots.
sections.details:
This study establishes practical online reinforcement learning design principles for real-world manipulation under large-scale domain randomization and sparse rewards.

- **Key Takeaways**: By pairing CTDE (treating the arm and gripper as distinct agents evaluated by a centralized critic) with HRA reward decomposition (simplifying value regression under visual noise), the framework simultaneously solves non-stationarity and critic gradient instability that plagued prior methods.

- **Future Directions**: The modular architecture is inherently suited for expansion to heterogeneous sensory inputs and higher actuator counts. Moving forward, the authors plan to scale this CTDE + HRA framework toward coordinated bimanual manipulation on humanoid robotic platforms.

takeaways: Separating arm (continuous SAC) and gripper (discrete SAC) action spaces while evaluating them jointly with a single centralized critic (CTDE) cleanly sidesteps environmental non-stationarity.
Because real-world RGB critic gradients easily destabilize, using HRA to split critic heads between sparse task achievement and dense potential-based grasping works remarkably well.

Even under realistic, broad workspaces (5-25x wider domain randomization), combining the right multi-agent architecture with modest human interventions (HIL) yields high-performing policies in about 2.5 hours.
limitations: Bootstrapping the initial policy still requires around 20 teleoperated human demonstrations, meaning it is not yet fully autonomous zero-shot learning.
Physical robot experiments were limited to single-arm setups; real-world validation of bimanual coordination or whole-body control (integrating humanoid locomotion) remains future work.
The grasping reward requires human engineering of potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) using gripper finger width and torque feedback.
